meta.title: Latin — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 38 sounds, spelling rules and patterns of endings — start here, beside Latin A1
meta.desc: How Latin is read and spelled, and how its words change their endings, before or beside the first word: 38 notes, one card each — 5 rules (the two pronunciations, the macron, where the stress falls, a doubled consonant, a vowel and m at the end of a word), the 8 vowels and diphthongs (a, e, i, o, u, ae, oe, au), 12 consonants that an English reader, or one of the two pronunciations, reads otherwise (c, g, gn, sc, ti, v, the consonant i, h, qu, r, s, ch), and 13 patterns of endings: the cases, the five declensions, a verb's four principal parts, the conjugations and a deponent verb. THERE ARE TWO PRONUNCIATIONS OF LATIN, and every card here gives both, the classical one first. The classical pronunciation is the one the macrons describe: the level decks print a macron over every long vowel (244 of Latin A1's 509 one-word headwords carry one), and in it c and g are always hard and v is a w. The Church pronunciation is the Italianate one: no long vowels, c and g soft before e and i, v as in English. They read 140 of those 509 headwords differently in at least one letter: v (60 headwords), c before e, i, ae or oe (30), g before the same (16), gn (6), sc before the same (4), ti before a vowel (8), ae and oe (11), h (17). WHAT THE SPEAKER READS, here and beside every word of the Latin decks: your device's ITALIAN voice, because almost no device has a Latin one, given the word without its macrons. So it gives the CHURCH value of every card of this deck — the second line — and never the classical one: it does not hold a long vowel, it softens c and g, and it says v. How it stresses a word is the voice's own doing and was not checked against the rule on the stress card. To learn the classical pronunciation, read the first line of the card and the first transcription beside each word, and say the word yourself; the speaker is the second. A device without an Italian voice is silent. THE CARDS: the front shows the letters, the rule or the ending. The back gives the classical sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet with the English sound it resembles, then the Church one, then the notes of the source, then words of the Latin A1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, and each word's two transcriptions from the dictionary, classical then Church (ˈ stands before the stressed syllable, ː after a long vowel, a dot between syllables). AND THE ENDINGS, which every sentence uses: a Latin noun changes its ending for its case and a verb for its person, and the level decks show the forms word by word, behind each card's All forms fold. The 13 cards here say what the patterns are — which declension ends how, what the four principal parts under a verb are for, how the conjugations differ — each beside the table of a Latin A1 card, copied from that card, so that the same table is met again on the word. THE ORDER is the rules, the vowels, the consonants, then the endings. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 4 days; it is meant to be studied beside Latin A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: nothing is written for this deck but its labels. Each sound and each English comparison is a cell of one row of the key named first below, placed as Classical or Church by the column its letter stands in there (h and ch, for which the key has no Church row, take theirs from the second page's table of the Church pronunciation); each note and each rule is a quoted run of one of the four pages. The letters both pronunciations read as an English reader expects (b, d, f, l, m, n, p, t, x) have no card, nor has y, which no A1 headword contains. The patterns show only forms an A1 card shows: there is no card for the adjectives' or the pronouns' declensions, whose tables are on their own cards (bonus, fortis, hic, ille, quī). — Sounds, English comparisons and notes: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Latin”, revision 1385934515 of 2026-11-16; Wikipedia, “Latin phonology and orthography”, revision 1381667996 of 2026-10-24. Endings: Wikipedia, “Latin declension”, revision 1385002572 of 2026-11-11; Wikipedia, “Latin conjugation”, revision 1367838080 of 2026-08-05 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, tables and meanings: the Latin A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: the classical pronunciation and the Church one
fields.Says: The charts below show the way in which the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) represents Classical Latin and Ecclesiastical Latin pronunciations in Wikipedia articles.Since the late 19th and early 20th centuries, an Italianate pronunciation of Latin has grown to be accepted as a universal standard in the Catholic Church.In Classical Latin, ⟨c g t⟩ are always pronounced hard, as [k g t]. In Ecclesiastical Latin, ⟨c g sc⟩ are pronounced as soft [tʃ dʒ ʃ] before the front vowels ⟨e i y ae oe⟩, and unstressed ⟨ti⟩ before a vowel is pronounced [tsi].

fields.Name: the macron: a long vowel
fields.Says: Classical Latin has long and short vowels. If vowel length is marked, long vowels are marked with macrons, ⟨ā, ē, ī, ō, ū, ȳ⟩, and short vowels with breves, ⟨ă, ĕ, ĭ, ŏ, ŭ, y̆⟩. Ecclesiastical Latin does not distinguish between long and short vowels.Textbooks and dictionaries usually indicate the length of vowels by putting a macron above the long vowel (less frequently, the breve is also used to mark short vowels), but it is not generally done in regular texts.

fields.Name: where the stress falls
fields.Says: In words of two syllables, the stress is on the first syllable. In words of three or more syllables, the stress is on the penultimate syllable if heavy, and on the antepenultimate syllable otherwise.Thus, a syllable is heavy if it ends in a long vowel, a diphthong, or a consonant.

fields.Name: the cases
fields.Says: A complete Latin noun declension includes up to seven grammatical cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, ablative and locative. The locative is limited to a few nouns: generally names of cities, small islands and a few other words.The nominative and vocative are always identical in the plural. […] The dative, ablative, and locative are always identical in the plural. […] For neuter nouns, the nominative, vocative, and accusative cases are always identical.

fields.Name: the second declension
fields.Says: The second declension is a large group of nouns consisting of mostly masculine nouns like equus, equī ('horse') and puer, puerī ('boy') and neuter nouns like castellum, castellī ('fort').In the nominative singular, most masculine nouns consist of the stem and the ending -us, although some end in -er, which is not necessarily attached to the complete stem.

fields.Says: The fourth declension is a group of nouns consisting of mostly masculine words such as flūctus, flūctūs m. ('wave') and portus, portūs m. ('port') with a few feminine exceptions, including manus, manūs f. ('hand') and domus, domūs f. ('house').

fields.Name: a verb's four principal parts
fields.Says: In a dictionary, Latin verbs are listed with four "principal parts" (or fewer for deponent and defective verbs), which allow the student to deduce the other conjugated forms of the verbs.the first person singular of the present indicative active […] the present infinitive active […] the first person singular of the perfect indicative active
